item.title: FRESCO: A Novel Consistency Control for Asynchronous Pipeline Parallel Training
item.description: arXiv:2611.11238v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism can accelerate distributed model training, but suffers from instability caused by inconsistent gradient computations. We identify a fundamental source of this inconsistency: error signals are coupled to forward-time features, not just parameter states. This means that parameters may evolve as long as they preserve forward-equivalence. Leveraging this insight, we introduce FRESCO, which frames asynchronous updates as a constrained optimization problem: it finds the minimal update modification that acts trivially on the activation subspace. We demonstrate that FRESCO consistently outperforms representative asynchronous baselines in LLM pre-training, with the gains most pronounced under deep pipelines and high inconsistency levels: at pipeline depth 32, it reaches the same loss as the strongest baseline with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time, while requiring 8~921$\times$ less memory overhead. Moving beyond the current limitations, FRESCO establishes a new foundation for high-utilization pipeline parallel training, providing a scalable path for large-model development on diverse, resource-constrained systems.
item.dc:creator: Dongyeop Lee, Namhoon Lee

item.title: AWS Serverless Infrastructure from WebAssembly Components
item.description: arXiv:2611.11293v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The infrastructure definitions and the code for serverless applications are often only loosely connected. This yields a large error class: the referenced infrastructure components might not exist. It is also hard to keep the application and its permissions in sync. To address this problem we present an infrastructure from code solution where we provision cloud infrastructure from Wasm Interface Type (WIT) - the language defining the interface of WebAssembly components. We limit ourselves to the basic example of an AWS Lambda function accessing S3 buckets. We build two interpreters for the WIT language: one that derives the definition of S3 buckets as infrastructure as code and least-privilege IAM permissions, and a generic runtime that runs the component as a Lambda function and provides access to the S3 buckets as capabilities. We formulate consistency properties that ensure the existence of the S3 buckets and correct permissions of the Lambda, and provide evidence that our interpreters satisfy them. We show how selected failures for deployment of such cloud components can be prevented using our technique and how a baseline setup fails at this task. Together with the strict sandboxing of the WebAssembly runtime we achieve an instance of capability-based security for access to AWS infrastructure as a further result.
item.dc:creator: Philipp Vollmer

item.title: A Per-Step Load-Balancing Engine for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.11402v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts serving, a layer finishes only when the most loaded GPU of its group does. Token routing shifts at every decode step and concentrates on a few experts, so most of the group's reserved GPU time waits on stragglers. Recovering that time means re-deciding, at every layer of every decode step, how each replicated expert's tokens divide between its copies. The exact linear-program solvers that make this decision optimally take longer than many of the layers they serve, and their working set outgrows GPU shared memory at deployment scale. We introduce Relief, a bidirectional pairwise relaxation that makes the linear program unnecessary, coming within a fraction of a point of the per-step optimum in a few passes of integer halving over the token counts. We build and measure three deployments, CUDA kernels on the serving GPU, the same verified engine on an FPGA over PCIe, and a fixed-function block beside the accelerator. On decode routing from three open MoE families, Relief holds the balance near the per-step optimum at every group size and layer time measured. Scored as effective utilization relative to that optimum, the kernel alone matches or exceeds every deployable scheme at every group size, from the hundred-microsecond layer on. The on-die engine widens that lead at every point, recovering up to 37.3 percentage points over the deployed static placement, while adding 0.02% of a current accelerator's transistors.
item.dc:creator: Jingyuan Li, Maolin Wang, Hayden So

item.title: MOMENT-DP: Momentum Aware Evaluation of Correlated Noise for Differentially Private Training
item.description: arXiv:2611.11457v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Temporally correlated noise can substantially improve the utility of differentially private optimization, yet candidate mechanisms are commonly designed or evaluated using only partial information about the optimization process, such as workload structure, learning-rate schedules, or local curvature. We study whether persistent optimizer state provides additional information that can change the relative utility of privacy-valid correlated-noise mechanisms. We introduce MOMENT-DP, an optimizer-state-aware framework that models how temporally correlated privacy noise propagates through momentum-based optimization. For locally quadratic objectives, MOMENT-DP expresses privacy-induced final loss through an optimizer transfer operator that jointly captures curvature, learning-rate scheduling, momentum, and temporal noise covariance. NoiseCurve's curvature-aware quadratic criterion is recovered exactly as the zero-momentum, constant-learning-rate special case. Changing only momentum while holding curvature, schedule, privacy calibration, and candidate mechanisms fixed induces genuine mechanism-ranking reversals. The effect persists outside exact quadratic dynamics in per-example-clipped private logistic regression, while remaining unresolved in the neural regime we study. These results establish optimizer state as an under-modeled, decision-relevant axis in evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise.
item.dc:creator: Sunny Gupta, Raja Viswanadha

item.title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.11910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.
item.dc:creator: Sina Barazandeh, Benjamin E. Lundell, Jose Lugo-Martinez

item.title: ShiftCache: Fast and Exact Indel Effect Prediction by Reusing Shifted Reference Encodings
item.description: arXiv:2611.11976v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sequence-to-function models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi read up to a megabase of DNA and score a genetic variant by comparing their predictions for the reference and alternate sequences. Insertions and deletions (indels) are costly to score, because an indel usually shifts the unchanged DNA after it onto a different pooling grid, which prevents direct reuse of the reference's encoder activations. The AlphaGenome Atlas scored more than 100 million indels with three full model passes each, although the DNA after an indel matches the reference shifted by the indel's length. We present ShiftCache, an exact reuse system that encodes each shifted reference once and shares it among all variants scored in the same window with the same shift. ShiftCache copies every encoder output a variant can reuse and recomputes the rest in batched tiles. On held-out AlphaGenome windows shared by many indels, in strict fp32 on one A6000, ShiftCache is 3.5 to 6.5$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6 to 2.7$\times$ faster than our adaptation of layer-by-layer reuse to indels. It is 3.5 to 4.1$\times$ faster than dense reimplementations of two published analyses with Borzoi and AlphaGenome, and 2.6$\times$ faster than dense execution with Enformer. Scoring each variant in its own centered 131 kb window makes ShiftCache only 1.36$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution, and highly diverse insertion lengths or many dispersed edits can make it slower than layer-by-layer reuse or dense execution. For encoders that meet our conditions, ShiftCache computes the same predictions as dense execution in exact arithmetic. On an A6000, every checked output of the default AlphaGenome and Borzoi runs matches dense execution within an absolute and relative tolerance of $10^{-5}$. With larger tile batches, with Enformer or on an H100, a small fraction of values exceeds this tolerance.
item.dc:creator: Sina Barazandeh, Arth Banka, Jose Lugo-Martinez

item.title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
item.description: arXiv:2611.12169v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.
item.dc:creator: Dongyang Geng, Haoqiong Bian, Zinuo Li, Haoyue Li

item.title: Lessons Not Learned: Why Cross-Chain Bridges Keep Losing Billions the Same Way
item.description: arXiv:2611.12252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bridge hacks have cost billions, often without exploiting a code bug. In the cross-chain bridge hacks we catalogue from 2021 to 2026, failures of security posture, meaning how a bridge's people, code, controls and off-chain infrastructure are set up, account for 88% of reported losses since 2023, and nearly all repeat earlier failures. Code audits cannot catch these failures, so we propose a bridge security assessment rubric. It scores each bridge deployment from on-chain evidence, and a hard cap drops the score to the lowest value when a fatal risk is present. A token is only as safe as its weakest deployment if all its deployments share one backing. For attacks nobody anticipated, we show that rate limits and an emergency stop still bound the loss. We build an analyzer that applies the rubric to deployed bridges and monitors them for changes, and an agentic analyzer that runs the same checks on any bridge. Operators learn what to fix, and users can compare bridges. Our rubric's controls cut bridge hack losses 105-fold, from \$3.52B to \$33M.
item.dc:creator: Mohsen Ahmadvand (Monad Foundation), Piotr Dobaczewski (Monad Foundation), Camille Bouzerand (Monad Foundation)

item.title: Reducing Provers in Distributed Quantum Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.12600v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur ($\mathsf{dQMA}$) model introduced by Fraigniaud, Le Gall, Nishimura, and Paz (ITCS 2021), a network of quantum computers verifies a global property with the aid of a quantum proof supplied by an untrusted prover. While the nodes are computationally unbounded, the challenge is to limit proof size and the communication required for verification. In this paper, we consider the model of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024), where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and define its extension to $k$ unentangled provers, denoted by $\mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$. In this setting, we investigate the proof size per node and the communication costs of reducing the number of provers. Our first result reduces the number of provers from $k$ to two, doubling the proof size without additional communication. Moreover, with four additional rounds, we can reduce the number of provers from $k$ to one, using at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Finally, we establish amplification for perfectly complete protocols. In this regime, a single prover suffices with a constant-factor overhead in our reductions, yielding $\mathsf{dQMAS} = \mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$.
item.dc:creator: Alex Della Schiava, Atsuya Hasegawa, Fran\c{c}ois Le Gall, Harumichi Nishimura

item.title: Flash-Fusion: Fast, Expressive Queries over Sensor Streams with LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2511.11885v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pervasive sensor deployments have generated significant interest in IoT data analysis across fields such as healthcare, transportation and urban planning. At the same time, the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a new tool for exploring IoT data through their expressive, natural language interface. Unfortunately, natural language querying of IoT sensor streams is impractical today: raw telemetry exhausts LLM context windows in fractions of a second at scale, incurs prohibitive per-token costs, and produces hallucinated responses. Existing systems work around these limits with lossy text summarization or unconstrained code synthesis, producing expensive, unverified computations. Multi-step queries compound this problem: logical errors in intermediate operations can derail the final answer. We present Flash-Fusion, an agentic framework for natural-language querying of tabular IoT data. Flash-Fusion identifies which available data fields and supported derivations can answer the user's query, constructs a plan using typed, domain-specific operators, and validates its structure and schema compatibility before executing. Because constructing plans still requires costly LLM reasoning, Flash-Fusion caches validated operator sequences for reuse across compatible queries. A smaller LLM adapts a cached plan's parameters to each query, cutting latency and cost. We evaluate Flash-Fusion across human activity recognition, ECG monitoring, and vehicular telematics, covering direct lookups, multi-step reasoning, predictive tasks, and out-of-scope requests. Flash-Fusion achieves 92.2% query accuracy versus 76.1% for ReAct, the strongest baseline, while completing queries 7x faster and consuming 5x fewer tokens. Flash-Fusion enables users across disciplines to explore IoT data without manually constructing queries.
item.dc:creator: Kausar Patherya, Ashutosh Dhekne, Francisco Romero

item.title: Leader Election via Unique Sink Orientation
item.description: arXiv:2511.19208v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A proof-labeling scheme (PLS) certifies a global property using only local checks. That is, a prover assigns a certificate to every node and each node accepts or rejects by inspecting only the certificates in its neighborhood, so that every graph satisfying some global property admits a certificate assignment accepted by all nodes (existence) and every certificate assignment accepted by all nodes gives a legal configuration (soundness). In this work, we design PLSs for two classical problems, leader certification and spanning tree certification, assuming that all nodes are anonymous, for a specific class of graphs. Certifying a unique leader is impossible in general anonymous graphs for any certificate size due to a well-known result for rings by [Korman, Kutten and Peleg, 2010]. This raises the question of which graph classes admit a PLS for leader certification with anonymous nodes, ideally with size independent of the size of the graph. Our work contributes to a growing list of such classes, which includes chordal graphs, meshed graphs and simply connected subsets of the triangular grid. We consider dismantlable graphs, a class which contains trees, chordal, bridged and Helly graphs, as well as the $k$-th powers of $\delta$-hyperbolic graphs for $k \geq 2\delta$. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first PLSs tailored to dismantlable graphs, potentially highlighting structural properties useful for certifying additional problems. Finally, we present a generic transformation that converts any labeling scheme with certificates of finite type into a silent self-stabilizing algorithm by adding only one extra state, assuming a Gouda fair scheduler, whereas known generic transformations require $O(\ell + \log n)$ bits for $\ell$-bit certificates. This transformation may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: J\'er\'emie Chalopin, Maria Kokkou

item.title: NAVIS: Concurrent Search and Update with Low Position-Seeking Overhead in On-SSD Graph-Based Vector Search
item.description: arXiv:2605.11523v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-disk graph-based vector search (GVS) has become the dominant approach for serving large-scale vector databases at high recall. Yet prior systems struggle to sustain concurrent search and update throughput on high-dimensional workloads. We identify the main bottleneck as position seeking, the graph traversal that finds neighbors during each update. Unlike search, which returns only the top-K closest vectors, it explores a much larger set to build an R-neighbor list of close neighbors and long-range shortcuts. These neighbors have different distance-accuracy requirements, yet search-oriented packed layouts fetch full vectors with every edge-list access, consuming cache capacity regardless of their role. We present NAVIS, an on-SSD GVS system that redesigns position seeking around this mismatch. At its core, locality-driven decoupling separates vectors from edgelists and packs graph-local edgelists together. This decoupling enables convergence-aware speculative reranking to selectively load full vectors until a sufficient set of close neighbors is resolved, while selecting the remaining shortcuts using approximate distances. It also allows NAVIS to devote cache capacity entirely to edgelists. To make this cache effective, NAVIS keeps the entrance graph fresh via lightweight updates that reuse traversal information already produced during position seeking, thereby maintaining a stable hot set of edgelists near its entry points. Across multiple large-scale benchmarks, NAVIS improves insertion throughput by up to 3.97x and concurrent search throughput by up to 4.00x while reducing search latency by up to 75.69%.
item.dc:creator: Jaeyong Song, Hongsun Jang, Changmin Shin, Seongyeon Park, Yong Jae Ryoo, Seo Jin Park, Jinho Lee

item.title: CIDERS: Cloud-Edge LLM Collaborative Learning via Accelerating Personalized Bilevel Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2609.15664v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Amid the rapid advancement of physical-world intelligence, cloud-edge collaborative large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising roadmap for practical LLM deployment. However, existing cloud-edge paradigms struggle to balance global consensus with local personalization, which fails to satisfy the need for a unified knowledge foundation on the cloud and domain-specific adaptation at the edge. To address this, we introduce, for the first time, a personalized bilevel optimization framework that formalizes cloud-edge LLM collaboration as a dual structure: the upper level optimizes edge-side personalization, while the lower level governs cloud-side knowledge transfer, reaching cloud-edge evolving in coordination. We then propose CIDERS, an efficient solver that decomposes the model into a learnable backbone and a messenger. While the cloud performs knowledge transfer to the learnable backbone, the key lies in embedding global trajectories into each local personalization step via consensus-variate correction to reconcile personalization with consensus. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis, including a geometric characterization of the local trajectory and a full convergence guarantee, revealing an explicit trade-off structure between personalization and global convergence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CIDERS consistently outperforms competitive baselines on the compressed edge path, with 3.1x and 1.7x gains on mathematical reasoning and code generation, respectively, and a 10\% relative gain on instruction metrics. Mechanism experiments attribute these gains to early consensus-corrected coordination and task-aware distillation. Overall, CIDERS offers a viable path toward consensus-guided continuous personalization in cloud-edge LLM systems.
item.dc:creator: Victor H. Chen, Hairui Yu, Stella K. Chung, Hong Yan

item.title: When Fancy Eviction Fails: Rethinking Cache Replacement For LLM Prefix Reuse
item.description: arXiv:2609.28870v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-running LLM applications and autonomous agents repeatedly send growing context, making prefix caching critical for reducing prefill cost. This raises a fundamental question: do decades of traditional cache-management techniques transfer directly to agentic and conversational LLM serving? We analyze production traces comprising over 20 billion processed tokens and evaluate 14 eviction algorithms across capacity-constrained HBM and large memory-pool settings. We find that simple Least Recently Used (LRU) is surprisingly robust, offering competitive performance against sophisticated traditional policies, though substantial headroom to Belady's optimum remains. The reason is structural: prefix reuse is dominated by the steady pacing of active sessions, making recency an unusually strong predictor for eviction. Nevertheless, prefix caching diverges from traditional workloads in ways that recency ignores, notably the prevalence of single-turn requests, extreme session footprint skew, and highly non-uniform miss costs because attention computation scales with token depth. To close the gap to optimality, we establish several design principles for prefix-cache management: keeping recency as the baseline while incorporating quick demotion to filter one-hit prompts, compute-aware eviction to prioritize expensive misses, and capacity-adaptive eviction granularity. Our traces and simulator are publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Yiyu Liu, Minlan Yu, Juncheng Yang

item.title: Seamless Reconfiguration for DAG-BFT (Technical Report)
item.description: arXiv:2610.00896v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Byzantine Atomic Broadcast in Asynchronous networks has been studied extensively for decades. In a fully asynchronous system with even one possible crash failure, the FLP impossibility result rules out deterministic consensus, motivating randomized protocols that achieve termination with probability one. More recently, DAG-Rider popularized a new abstraction in which processes continuously reliably broadcast blocks to construct a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and then locally derive a total order using a randomized perfect coin. This separation of dissemination from ordering has renewed interest in asynchronous DAG-based Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) and inspired numerous protocols that improve expected latency or throughput. Reconfiguration, however, remains largely unexplored. Existing DAG-based BFT protocols generally assume a static set of processes, whereas deployed systems must occasionally add or remove nodes in response to operational demands. Existing solutions are not seamless; they either pause the system or delay membership changes until a predetermined epoch boundary. This may be impractical and can introduce downtime. A single agreed switching round is difficult to use seamlessly: by the time processes learn it, the dissemination layer may already have advanced beyond it. In this work, we present a seamless reconfiguration protocol for Asynchronous DAG-based Byzantine Atomic Broadcast. Our protocol allows the DAG to continue growing while the membership and corresponding quorum thresholds change, without halting the system. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first protocol to provide seamless reconfiguration for DAG-based Byzantine atomic broadcast in a fully asynchronous network.
item.dc:creator: Michael Yiqing Hu, Leander Jehl, Paul Franke-Bergmann, Jialin Li, Christian Berger

item.title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.08864v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by output-length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while reducing fluctuations in the supply of generated samples to the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Within our asynchronous architecture, ASP's scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. The complete system improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. It also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.
item.dc:creator: Salah Chikhi, Luis Zuin, Entong Li, Zeng Li

item.title: CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data
item.description: arXiv:2208.03784v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: There is growing awareness that the analysis of personal data, such as individuals' mobility, financial, and health data, can provide significant benefits to society. However, liberal societies have so far refrained from such analytics, arguably due to the lack of secure analytics platforms that scale to billions of records while operating in a very strong threat model. We contend that one fundamental gap here is the lack of an architecture that can scale (actively-)secure multi-party computation (MPC) horizontally without weakening security. To bridge this gap, we present CoVault, an analytics platform that leverages server-aided MPC and trusted execution environments (TEEs) to colocate the MPC parties in a single datacenter without reducing security, and scales MPC horizontally to the datacenter's available resources. CoVault scales well empirically. For example, CoVault can scale the DualEx 2PC protocol to perform epidemic analytics for a country of 80M people (about 11.85B data records/day) on a continuous basis using one core pair for every 30,000 people.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: In Proceedings of the 34th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 25), pp. 567-586, USENIX Association, 2025
item.dc:creator: Roberta De Viti, Isaac Sheff, Noemi Glaeser, Baltasar Dinis, Rodrigo Rodrigues, Bobby Bhattacharjee, Anwar Hithnawi, Deepak Garg, Peter Druschel

item.title: The Smart Buildings Control Suite: A Diverse Open Source Benchmark to Evaluate and Scale HVAC Control Policies for Sustainability
item.description: arXiv:2410.03756v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Commercial buildings account for 17\% of U.S. carbon emissions, with roughly half of that from Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC). HVAC devices form a complex thermodynamic system, and while model predictive control and reinforcement learning have been used to optimize control policies, scaling to thousands of buildings remains a significant unsolved challenge. Most current approaches are over-optimized for specific buildings and rely on proprietary data or hard-to-configure simulators. We present the Smart Buildings Control Suite, the first open source interactive HVAC control benchmark with a focus on solutions that generalize across building. It has 3 components: real-world data from 11 buildings over 6 years, a lightweight data-driven simulator, and a modular Physically Informed Neural Network (PINN) building model. The buildings span multiple climates, management systems, and sizes, and both the simulator and PINN easily transfer to new buildings, ensuring solutions using this benchmark are robust to these factors and only reliant on fully scalable building models. This represents a major step towards scaling HVAC optimization from the lab to buildings everywhere. To facilitate use, our benchmark is compatible with the Gym standard, and our data is available at our webpage. Code at https://github.com/google/sbsim
item.dc:creator: Judah Goldfeder, Victoria Dean, Zixin Jiang, Xuezheng Wang, Bing dong, Hod Lipson, John Sipple

item.title: Lazy Qubit Reordering for Accelerating Parallel State-Vector-based Quantum Circuit Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2410.04252v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This article proposes two quantum operation scheduling methods for accelerating parallel state-vector-based quantum circuit simulation using multiple graphics processing units (GPUs). The proposed methods reduce all-to-all communication caused by qubit reordering, which can dominate the overhead of parallel simulation. Our out-of-order approach eliminates redundant reorderings by introducing intentional delays in reordering communications such that multiple reorderings can be aggregated into a single reordering. The delays are carefully introduced based on the principles of time-space tiling, or a cache optimization technique for classical computers, which we use to arrange the execution order of quantum operations. Moreover, we develop these methods tailored for two primary procedures in variational quantum eigensolver simulation: quantum state update (QSU) and expectation value computation (EVC). Our QSU simulation takes an advantage of the hierarchical interconnection of GPU systems to avoid slow inter-node communication. On the other hand, our EVC simulation reduces the number of reorderings by diagonalization of Pauli strings. Experimental validation on 32-GPU executions demonstrates acceleration in QSU and EVC$\unicode{x2014}$up to 54$\times$ and 1,657$\times$, respectively$\unicode{x2014}$compared to an inorder-based method. We believe that our out-of-order approach is useful for accelerating large-scale quantum circuit simulations, including QSU and/or EVC that operate qubits in a regular manner.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing 6(4), Article 27, 1-33 (2025)
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Teranishi, Shoma Hiraoka, Wataru Mizukami, Masao Okita, Fumihiko Ino

item.title: Accelerating AIGC Services with Latent Action Diffusion Scheduling in Edge Networks
item.description: arXiv:2412.18212v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) has gained significant popularity for creating diverse content. However, current AIGC models primarily focus on content quality within a centralized framework, resulting in a high service delay and negative user experiences. The workload of an AIGC task is determined by model complexity and multi-layered encoder architectures, posing significant challenges for its modeling, deployment, and scheduling within resource-constrained edge networks. We model an offloading problem among edges for providing real AIGC services and propose \textbf{LAD-TS}, a novel Latent Action Diffusion-based Task Scheduling method that orchestrates multiple edge servers for expedited AIGC services by leveraging the diffusion model's conditional guidance capability and the reinforcement learning's environment interaction ability. We first design an innovative Latent Action Diffusion Network (LADN) model based on traditional diffusion models. We then incorporate the LADN model into deep reinforcement learning, forming an effective LAD-TS method for task scheduling in distributed edge networks. Meanwhile, we design a latent action diffusion strategy to achieve near-optimal decisions quickly by utilizing historical action probabilities instead of Gaussian noise. Furthermore, we implement a refined AIGC model and develop \textbf{DEdgeAI}, a prototype edge system with the refined AIGC model deployment to evaluate our LAD-TS method. DEdgeAI provides a real AIGC service for users, demonstrating up to $7.36\%-18.11\%$ and $34.07\%-94.96\%$ shorter service delays than the state-of-the-art methods and representative commercial platforms, respectively. We release our open-source code at https://github.com/ChangfuXu/DEdgeAI/
item.dc:creator: Changfu Xu, Jianxiong Guo, Wanyu Lin, Haodong Zou, Yuzhu Liang, Xiaowen Chu, Jiannong Cao, Tian Wang

item.title: MUSE: Multi-Tenant Model Serving With Seamless Model Updates
item.description: arXiv:2602.11776v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In binary classification systems, decision thresholds translate model scores into actions. Choosing suitable thresholds relies on the specific distribution of the underlying model scores but also on the specific business decisions of each client using that model. However, retraining models inevitably shifts score distributions, invalidating existing thresholds. In multi-tenant Score-as-a-Service environments, where decision boundaries reside in client-managed infrastructure, this creates a severe bottleneck: recalibration requires coordinating threshold updates across hundreds of clients, consuming excessive human hours and leading to model stagnation. We introduce MUSE, a model serving framework that enables seamless model updates by decoupling model scores from client decision boundaries. Designed for multi-tenancy, MUSE optimizes infrastructure re-use by sharing models via dynamic intent-based routing, combined with a two-level score transformation that maps model outputs to a stable, reference distribution. Deployed at scale by Feedzai, MUSE processes over a thousand events per second, and over 55 billion events in the last 12 months, across several dozens of tenants, while maintaining high-availability and low-latency guarantees. By reducing model lead time from weeks to minutes, MUSE promotes model resilience against shifting attacks, saving millions of dollars in fraud losses and operational costs.

item.title: Vectorized Dynamic Histograms for Sparse Oblique Forests
item.description: arXiv:2603.00326v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse oblique (SPO), part of the top-ranked configuration of Google's Yggdrasil Decision Forests (YDF), improve the accuracy while maintaining interpretability of Random Forests (RF) and Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT) by scanning a sparse linear combination of features instead of a single feature. Because projections are sampled at runtime, training is significantly slower, as pre-run optimizations such as presorting cannot be used. We overhaul SPO training in YDF, first by fixing inefficiencies in the released version, achieving 2-5x speedup, then by devising two novel methods, one aimed at GBTs and the other at RFs: (1) Hierarchical AVX2 and AVX-512-vectorized histogram filling speeds up typical GBT-depth trees by up to 1.6x in SPO-GBT and 2x for SPO-RF, and (2) runtime-dynamic histograms between vectorized histograms and exact splits, speeds up deeper, RF depth-typical trees (depths 16 to purity) by up to 1.6x with no detectable effect on accuracy. Our optimizations bring SPO-RF training time on par with YDF's axis-aligned RF. We extensively evaluate on 8 natural and 11 synthetic datasets of up to 10.5 million rows and 1.6 million features, from depth 6 to purity, and open-source the implementation.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Lubonja, Jungsang Yoon, Haoyin Xu, Yue Wan, Yilin Xu, Richard Stotz, Mathieu Guillame-Bert, Joshua T. Vogelstein, Randal Burns

item.title: Benchmarking Quantum Computers via Protocols, Comparing Superconducting and Ion-Trap Quantum Technology
item.description: arXiv:2603.27397v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Both Superconducting and Ion-Trap are leading quantum architectures common in the current landscape of the quantum computing field, each with distinct characteristics and operational constraints. Understanding and measuring the underlying $\underline{\text{quantumness}}$ of these devices is essential for assessing their readiness for practical applications and guiding future progress and research. Building on earlier work (Meirom, Mor and Weinstein Arxiv 2505.12441), we utilize a benchmarking strategy applicable for comparing these two architectures by measuring "quantumness" directly on optimal sub-chips. Distinct from existing metrics, our approach employs rigorous binary fidelity thresholds derived from the classical limits of state transfer. This enables us to definitively establish quantum advantage of a designated sub-region. Here we apply this quality assurance methodology to platforms from both technologies. This comparison provides a protocol-based evaluation of quantumness advantage, revealing not only the strengths and weaknesses of each tested chip and its sub-chips but also offering a common language for their assessment. By abstracting away technical differences in the final result, we demonstrate a benchmarking strategy that bridges the gap between disparate quantum-circuit technologies, enabling fair performance comparisons and establishing a critical foundation for evaluating future claims of quantum advantage. We encourage other companies to emulate the independent qubit availability and the fair pricing, as do IBM and AQT, which allow researchers to perform such assessments. In the discussion section, we consider an important future direction of using "benchmarking via protocols" also for fault-tolerant quantum computing with logical qubits.
item.dc:creator: Nitay Mayo, Tal Mor, Yossi Weinstein

item.title: Cooperate to Compete: Strategic Data Generation and Incentivization Framework for Coopetitive Cross-Silo Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2604.14886v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In data-sensitive domains such as finance, cross-silo federated learning (CFL) allows organizations to collaboratively train AI models without sharing raw data. However, many practical CFL deployments are coopetitive, where organizations cooperate during model training while competing in downstream markets. In such settings, training contributions can improve the global model yet inadvertently strengthen rivals, eroding one's competitive advantage. This dilemma is amplified by non-IID data, which leads to asymmetric learning gains and undermines sustained participation. While existing work reward organizations based on marginal training contributions, they fail to account for the implicit costs of strengthening competitors. In this paper, we introduce CoCoGen+, a coopetition-compatible data generation and incentivization framework that jointly models data heterogeneity and inter-organizational competition while endogenizing GenAI-based synthetic data generation as a strategic decision. Specifically, CoCoGen+ formulates each training round as a weighted potential game, where organizations strategically decide how much data to generate by balancing learning gains against computational costs and utility losses caused by competition. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the continuous Nash equilibrium under the adopted model and develop a provably convergent scalar bisection algorithm. We further analyze how bilateral payoff redistribution modifies residual competition and data-generation incentives, and empirically evaluate the social welfare and individual utilities of the resulting allocations. Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 validate the feasibility of CoCoGen+. The results show how heterogeneity, competition intensity, and incentives shape organizational strategies and social welfare, while CoCoGen+ achieves higher social welfare than competition-aware baselines.

item.title: Parallel-in-Time Training of Recurrent Neural Networks for Dynamical Systems Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2605.12683v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reconstructing nonlinear dynamical systems (DS) from data (DSR) is a fundamental challenge in science and engineering, but it inherently relies on sequential models. Recent breakthroughs for sequential models have produced algorithms that parallelize computation along sequence length $T$, achieving logarithmic time complexity, $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$. Since sequence lengths have been practically limited due to the linear runtime complexity $\mathcal{O}(T)$ of classical backpropagation through time, this opens new avenues for DSR. This paper studies two prominent classes of parallel-in-time algorithms for this task, both of which leverage parallel associative scans as their core computational primitive. The first class comprises models with linear yet non-autonomous dynamics and a nonlinear readout, such as modern State Space Models (SSMs), while the second consists of general nonlinear models which can be parallelized using the DEER framework. We find that the linear training-time recurrence of the first class of models imposes limitations that often hinder learning of accurate nonlinear dynamics. To address this, we augment DEER with Generalized Teacher Forcing (GTF), a novel variant within the more general nonlinear framework that ensures stable and effective learning of nonlinear dynamics across arbitrary sequence lengths. Using GTF-DEER, we investigate the benefits of training on extremely long sequences ($T$ approaching $10^5$) for DSR. Our results show that access to such long trajectories significantly improves DSR if the data features long time scales. This work establishes GTF-DEER as a robust tool for data-driven discovery and underscores the largely untapped potential of long-sequence learning in modeling complex DS.
item.dc:creator: Florian Hess, Florian G\"otz, Daniel Durstewitz

item.title: PithTrain: A Compact and Agent-Native MoE Training System
item.description: arXiv:2605.31463v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the dominant architecture for frontier language models. To meet this demand, production frameworks have built optimized MoE training stacks over years of engineering effort. Yet evolving these stacks for new architectures and system optimizations remains expensive. With the rise of AI coding agents, they could automate parts of training-framework development and accelerate this evolution. But applying them to these existing frameworks carries hidden costs, invisible to today's throughput-only evaluations. We name this missing dimension agent-task efficiency (ATE): the cost of using coding agents to understand, operate, and extend a framework. Grounded in four agent-native design principles, we build PithTrain, a compact, agent-native MoE training framework supporting pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. We further introduce ATE-Bench, covering real-world training-framework tasks. Our evaluation shows PithTrain achieves throughput competitive with production frameworks and higher agent-task efficiency on ATE-Bench. On new-feature tasks, PithTrain uses up to 62% fewer Agent Turns than Megatron-LM, and up to 44% and 64% less Active GPU Time than Megatron-LM and TorchTitan, respectively.

item.title: Improved Scaling for Fast Mode of Ozaki Scheme II
item.description: arXiv:2606.29129v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ozaki scheme II emulates high-precision matrix multiplication using low-precision integer matrix operations based on the Chinese remainder theorem (CRT). It first scales the high-precision matrices to convert them into integer matrices. For this scaling step, Ozaki scheme II provides two modes: accurate mode, which uses INT8 matrix multiplication to estimate scaling factors, and fast mode, which applies the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality at lower computational cost. We show that the existing formula lacks scale invariance; multiplying the input matrices by a constant changes the effective bit width of the integer matrices in the scaling step, causing accuracy degradation or CRT recovery failure. To address this, we propose a revised scaling formula derived from the CRT uniqueness condition via the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. The proposed formula is scale-invariant by construction, guarantees that the CRT uniqueness condition is always satisfied, and introduces no additional overhead over the original fast mode. Experiments on an NVIDIA GH200 GPU show that the proposed method achieves accuracy comparable to that of accurate mode while maintaining throughput comparable to that of fast mode. In the accuracy--throughput trade-off, the proposed method overcomes the accuracy limitation of fast mode and the throughput constraint of accurate mode, offering a superior accuracy and performance.
item.dc:creator: Shota Kawakami, Daisuke Takahashi

item.title: DDBench: A Benchmark for Agentic Debugging on Distributed Systems
item.description: arXiv:2608.14863v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-based coding agents have advanced rapidly on single-process SWE tasks, with frontier models now clustering in the high-70s on SWE-bench Verified. Distributed-system debugging, however, remains an under-explored regime: bugs span processes, nodes, and protocol interactions, with root causes rarely recoverable from source alone and brute-force exploration intractable across non-deterministic interleavings. This leaves two gaps in LLM and agent evaluation: no code-repair benchmark targets distributed-system bugs, and no controlled study isolates how much externally provided debugging context changes agent success on them. We introduce DDBench, a code-repair benchmark of 60 historical bugs mined from 13 open-source distributed systems, partitioned into three reasoning-scope tiers. DDBench evaluates every case under two matched conditions: a symptom-only condition where the agent receives only the bug symptom and repository, and a context-augmented condition where it additionally receives bounded debugging context (logs, traces, runtime state, and targeted code-investigation notes), isolating the effect of debugging context from model capability. The evaluation of 10 LLMs on DDBench reveals several findings. First, distributed debugging exercises a reasoning dimension that single-process benchmarks do not surface: models' pass rates span 45 pp, and pairwise bootstrap separates 6 of 15 top-tier model pairs at p < 0.05 on DDBench's hardest case-set. Second, bounded debugging context lifts aggregate pass rate by +19.0 pp, and the lift is asymmetric: weaker models gain more in pass rate, while stronger models gain more in efficiency. Third, debugging context requires careful curation, as even faithful debugging context can anchor a strong model on the wrong layer of the system when its observation sits far from the fault.

item.title: Catching the Rug: Early Prediction of Fraudulent Memecoins on Solana via Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.20271v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid proliferation of memecoins on blockchain platforms has increased the risk of fraudulent activities, particularly rug pulls. While previous studies have focused on Ethereum-based tokens, this paper shifts the spotlight to Solana, the leading blockchain for memecoins by trading volume and token count. Unlike Ethereum, where rug pulls often exploit smart contract backdoors, Solana memecoin rug pulls are predominantly driven by liquidity manipulation and social dynamics. This research pioneers large-scale rug pull early detection in the Solana ecosystem by assembling a dataset of 6.4 million tokens over 7 months. Market analysis reveals that a vast majority of these memecoins exhibit rug pull characteristics within one hour of launch, highlighting the urgency of short-horizon prediction. Despite the absence of code-level features, we demonstrate that classic machine learning models, particularly Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), achieve robust performance in detecting potential rug pulls using only the first 5 minutes of trading data. Furthermore, we evaluate cross-platform generalization between PumpFun and Raydium, revealing that multi-source data fusion significantly mitigates domain shift and improves detection reliability. This study advances the understanding of DeFi fraud on high-throughput chains and provides a practical framework for protecting investors.
item.dc:creator: Jianghai Li, Pavel Kuznetsov, Yury Yanovich, Konstantin Nott-Whaley, Igor Vodolazov

item.title: Distributed Linear Programming on GPU Clusters at Extreme Scale
item.description: arXiv:2609.09108v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large linear programs can exceed the memory of a single compute node. Although first-order methods replace sparse factorizations with GPU-suited matrix-vector products, other solver phases can reintroduce a single-node memory limit. We present SHARDLP, a distributed GPU LP solver that keeps the matrix and primal-dual state partitioned from sharded input through solution output. On the Google PDLP benchmark, SHARDLP solves ten of eleven instances, compared with eight in the published CPU PDLP study. On the largest benchmark, eight H200 GPUs solve a 1.185-billion-variable, 6.338-billion-nonzero LP in 9.9 minutes; the published CPU experiment reports 21.06 hours on different hardware. Beyond this benchmark, separately checked multi-node solves reach up to 13.604 billion variables and 40.807 billion nonzeros, while validated executions span up to 76 GPUs across 29 compute nodes. For column-partitioned solves, support-aware communication skips GPUs that store no coefficients for a row; on an LP with 2.76 billion nonzeros, it cuts modelled communication by 92.97% and improves solver time by 1.27x-1.52x. The code for SHARDLP is available at https://github.com/ArnaudDeza/ShardLP.
item.dc:creator: Arnaud Deza, Santanu S. Dey, Pascal Van Hentenryck

item.title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.01077v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.
item.dc:creator: Baran Atalar, Selly Beyene, Xutong Liu, Carlee Joe-Wong

item.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
item.description: arXiv:2611.03523v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Jiang, Chenglin Liu, John Rose, Mason Miller, Ruthesh Thavamani, Juntao Wu, Yinwei Huang, Jiahao Xu, Peng Huang

item.title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.09424v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as BF16 and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52x and 1.48x over the fastest baseline on an RTX 4060 Ti and an RTX 5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43 bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.
item.dc:creator: Emil Sch\"atzle, Markus P\"uschel
